FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim checks out against the letter: Henry's first letter home, the 34th New York's arrival at Washington via Baltimore, the twenty men detailed with loaded guns "in case of attack," the city's tepid "rather cheered" reception, the bullet holes in the depot roof from an earlier disturbance, the declined furlough on cost grounds, and the eight dollars sent home to his widowed mother. The "earlier row" framing for the bullet holes is a reasonable period-faithful reading.

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, well-grounded draft that earns its length and stays vivid. It nails the historical hook — a brand-new regiment's first passage through Baltimore, the very city where the 6th Massachusetts had been mobbed and bloodied that April, which is exactly why twenty men marched with loaded weapons and why the depot still bore bullet holes. The summary lets a knowing reader feel that tension without importing the outside event (per the no-outside-events rule), and the "rather cheered" detail is a lovely, precise period note that complicates the expected hostility. The human beat — declining the furlough so his mother keeps the eight dollars — lands naturally and is woven, not tacked on. Minor calibration: "an earlier row" slightly undersells; the letter's own language and the loaded-gun detail signal real, recent danger, so a word like "earlier trouble" or "earlier clash" carries the menace a hair better without spoiling or importing. The phrase "Already mindful of his widowed mother" is a touch editorial-explanatory; the act itself already shows the mindfulness. Both are polish, not problems.

old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.

The draft correctly does NOT name Bull Run/Manassas or the battle's outcome — Henry himself does not name it or know the result, so importing it would violate the only-facts-in-this-letter rule. FEEDBACK: This is strong and period-honest. The standout virtue, from a historian's lens, is that it captures exactly what makes this letter significant — a Union soldier in the capital hearing the guns of the war's first major battle in real time, before anyone knew it would become a rout — without spoiling that Henry himself cannot name. Letting his estimate and his own words carry the scene is the right call. Two refinements: (1) "a real-time eyewitness account of distant fighting" is slightly redundant tail-matter and a touch clinical; the quote already establishes the real-time eyewitness quality, so that clause can be tightened or folded in. Strictly, it's an "ear-witness" account — he hears cannon, he does not see the field — and "eyewitness" mildly overclaims; "hears the war arrive" or "by ear" is more precise. (2) The piece slightly buries the milestone stakes: a historian connecting dots wants the signal that THIS is the opening of the shooting war, conveyed through Henry's vantage rather than asserted. The faith beat and chapel detail are well woven and earn their place; keep them. Length is fine and the voice is warm without sentimentality.

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is supported by this letter: Washington, D.C. dateline; recipient Frances ("sister" per metadata); five hours of daily drill; the Colonel telling each Captain the men were improving (the "praise"); two newspapers to read; the request for one dollar to wash a shirt; the postscript "We are ordered off"; "There has been a hard battle today"; and the reversal "You need not send any money now, till I write." Nothing from outside the letter (Bull Run, panic, Maryland) has leaked into the draft text — correct restraint, since the letter itself names no battle.

FEEDBACK: Strong and faithful. The draft nails the editorial spine of this letter — the whiplash between mundane camp routine and the intruding postscript — which is exactly why this letter matters: it is a private, real-time fragment of the day First Bull Run was fought, written by a soldier who does not yet know what has happened ("Have not heard much about it yet"). The draft honors the hard rule by NOT naming Bull Run, and that's the right call for the summary text. Two small notes. First, "fills most of this letter... with ordinary camp life" is accurate but slightly undersells one period-telling detail you have room to surface: Henry's vow about guard duty ("They will never find me sleeping while on guard") — a green soldier's earnestness that lands as poignant once the war arrives mid-letter. Second, the dramatic engine of the postscript is partly that Henry reports the battle as a same-day rumor he can't yet interpret; "a hard battle was fought that day" is fine, but you can sharpen the stakes by signaling he writes in the dark. Length sits around 360 characters — appropriate for the rich style. The draft is publishable as-is; the suggestion below only tightens the human beat.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and disciplined work. The military restraint is exactly right: a historian's instinct would be to write "as news of Bull Run reached Washington," but Henry plainly does not know what battle it was, so importing the name would violate the letter's own epistemic horizon — and the draft resists that temptation. What the letter actually shows, and what the draft captures well, is the soldier's-eye view of July 21, 1861: a man in the capital who can hear that "a hard battle today" has occurred but has "not heard much about it yet." That fog-of-war immediacy is the real military value here, and it's worth making the dating slightly more legible. The draft never states the letter's date or that this is the eve of the regiment moving out; "We are ordered off" plus the battle is precisely the mobilization moment, and a reader connecting dots benefits from the temporal anchor. The phrase "fills most of this letter" is accurate and the whiplash structure is well rendered. Minor: "request for a dollar to wash a shirt" slightly compresses two separate lines (he asks for a dollar; separately wants a shirt washed) — fine for a summary. Length sits around 360 characters, within target.

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim checks out against the letter: Washington, D.C. dateline; the regiment stationed as guards to keep rebels from crossing the river; the overheard opinion that the regiment "may never see a battle"; Henry's "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where"; the five-dollar gold piece sent home by the Capt. with the "I put that down as a command" order to his sister and mother to use the money; and the Co. H private shot when soldiers were playing with their guns, the third such death by carelessness. Note: the letter never names the "34th New York" — that unit identity is imported from collection metadata, not stated in this letter. Per the brief's hard rule ("invent nothing beyond this letter"), the regiment number is technically outside the letter text, though it is the correct unit and arguably permissible grounding. Flagging it so you can decide; everything else is fully supported.

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, vivid draft that earns its length and lands the three best beats of the letter — the guard-duty stasis, the gold piece with its tender "command," and the accidental death. The voice is period-appropriate and warm without sentimentality. Two refinements worth weighing. First, the unit name: "34th New York regiment" is accurate to the collection but not to this letter; if the project wants strict per-letter sourcing, soften to "his regiment." If grounding-by-known-fact is acceptable, keep it. Second, the draft omits the single most resonant period detail of the letter's opening — Henry's illness and his fear of "fever and ague" from sleeping on the ground, which foreshadows the disease that killed more Civil War soldiers than combat. That human-and-historical beat is arguably more significant than the gold-piece anecdote and is currently absent. The escape is plainly the strongest hook and it is over-told: "feigned illness to hoard his daily opium, then drugged his guard's coffee and slipped through three enemy regiments" spends the whole payoff in the tooltip, leaving a reader nothing to discover in the letter itself. That violates the brief's "tease the stakes; do not flatly spoil the payoff." The stabbing and the inspection, crammed into a trailing sentence, read as a topic-list ("Henry also reports... and Brig. Gen. Gormon's inspection") — exactly the tacked-on enumeration the brief warns against. The human texture is present but mechanical. I would lead with the escape, hold back the method, anchor it to Kellogg's known captivity, and let the camp killing stand as the second beat for contrast — the war's danger arriving not from the enemy but from within Henry's own camp. Drop or compress the inspection unless it carries weight the letter gives it. But none of this can be finalized until the transcription is read.

SUGGESTED: (Offered provisionally, pending fact-check — names, numbers, and the "sharp shooters" detail must be confirmed against the letter before use.) Henry recounts an audacious escape from rebel hands: a soldier captured in the same fight as Kellogg quietly worked his way free of his captors and back to Union lines — and brings word that Kellogg himself is alive and held at Richmond. FACT ISSUES: Two misstatements. Minor, defensible, but tightening it would be safer. (2) "lately dubbed 'the sharp shooters' in the papers" — the letter says "I see in the papers we are called the sharp shooters"; "lately" is an invented time qualifier. Drop it. Also note "Gormon" is spelled exactly that way in the source (people array and transcription both say "Gormon"), so the draft preserves it correctly — keep it. Everything else (feigned illness, hoarded daily opium, drugged the guard's coffee, Kellogg held unwounded at Richmond, taken in the same skirmish, drunken stabbing, victim died by morning, Gormon's inspection of the regiment) is supported. The draft omits two arguably notable beats — Henry's homesickness/the farm faltering with him gone and James in school — but omission isn't a fact error.

FEEDBACK: The lead is well chosen — the opium escape is genuinely the most cinematic true detail in the letter, and the draft is right to open on it. The prose is vivid and earns most of its length. Problems are mechanical, not editorial: the sentence is a single 60-word run-on chained by colons and dashes, which strains readability in a tooltip. "confirms Kellogg is held unwounded" is good, but "in the same skirmish as Kellogg" front-loads a name before the reader knows who Kellogg is. The Gormon/sharp-shooters clause is fine but feels tacked on at the tail; the stabbing and the inspection are two unrelated beats stacked with "also," which flattens them. Trim "lately," reconsider "slipped through," and break the monster sentence. The draft is strong enough that I'd sharpen rather than replace.

Every claim is anchored in the letter: Camp McClellan, Poolesville "about three miles from our camp," the eight rebels who "came across to our side as deserters" reporting "the rebels have nothing to eat," the journal abandoned "since it has been so cold" and his regret, and the wish to attend the sing school back home. "Near Poolesville" is a fair, supported paraphrase of the three-miles line. One small note, not an error: the recipient is Henry's sister Frances, and the draft's "be home for the village sing school" lightly compresses the letter's actual phrasing ("I should like to attend if I was at home") — accurate in spirit.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and period-correct. The summary correctly elevates the right anchor: eight Confederate deserters crossing the lines reporting the enemy "has nothing to eat" is the historically significant beat — genuine soldier's-eye intelligence on Confederate supply shortages along the upper Potomac in the first winter of the war, before such hardship was widely assumed. Framing it as "a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac" is exactly the right register: it tells a historian why the letter matters without overclaiming. The human turn — the abandoned journal in the cold, the ache for the village sing school — is woven in, not tacked on, and earns the rich-style length. The voice is warm without sentimentality. Two minor refinements: "With little else to tell" is a touch listless to hinge the second sentence on; Henry's own framing ("everything goes on here about the same from day to day") is the more vivid winter-quarters note if you want to gesture at the monotony. And the letter is to his sister Frances — not load-bearing for the summary, but the homesickness reads warmer knowing the audience. The draft does not need a rewrite; it earns its length and stays accurate.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his sister from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry reports eight rebels crossing the lines as deserters who say the enemy has nothing to eat — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the upper Potomac in the war's first winter. With everything "about the same from day to day," he confesses he has let his journal lapse in the cold, and admits he'd give much to be home for the village sing school.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every military-relevant claim in the draft is grounded in the letter: the location "Camp McClellan," the eight rebels who "came across to our side as deserters," their report that "the rebels have nothing to eat," the discontinued journal "since it has been so cold," and the sing school Henry wishes he could attend. Poolesville being about three miles from camp supports "near Poolesville" (the draft says "near," not the exact distance, so no misstatement). Nothing about unit, rank, date, or outcome is invented or distorted.

FEEDBACK: Militarily this is sound and well-judged. The draft correctly identifies the load-bearing fact — eight Confederate deserters crossing the lines and reporting the enemy is out of food — and correctly frames it as a soldier's-eye intelligence detail about Confederate supply distress along the Potomac in winter 1861. That is exactly the right emphasis: this letter's historical value is the desertion/starvation observation, not the camp routine. Good restraint in not importing the regiment (34th NY) or any battle context the letter doesn't mention. Two small notes. First, "crossing the lines as deserters and saying" is slightly clunky; "came across as deserters, reporting..." reads cleaner and stays faithful. Second, the human beat (stopped journal in the cold, longing for the village sing school) is appropriate and earns its place — winter-quarters monotony is genuine context here. The draft is already strong and within the target length; only light polish is warranted.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, about three miles from Poolesville, Henry passes along the day's news: eight rebels came across the lines as deserters, reporting the enemy has nothing to eat — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac in the winter of 1861. With camp life otherwise unchanged from day to day, he confesses he has let his journal lapse in the cold, and admits he'd give much to be home for the village sing school.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is anchored in this letter — Camp McClellan, Poolesville (~3 miles off), the eight rebels crossing as deserters and reporting the enemy "have nothing to eat," the abandoned journal in the cold, the wish to be home for the sing school. The draft does not import the December 1861 supply context that the editorial note speculates about; it keeps to the soldier's own report. Good discipline.

FEEDBACK: This is strong, vivid, and faithful — the hook earns its place. "A soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac" is exactly the kind of historian's framing that justifies the length without inventing anything. Two small craft notes. First, the recipient is missing: this is a letter to his sister Frances, and naming her would deepen the closing human beat (the homesickness is addressed TO someone, not broadcast). Second, the draft skips the single freshest human detail in the letter — Henry has gotten an accordion and is being taught to play it by Bill Robers. That domestic, slightly comic note ("I have not made much progress yet") is the texture of winter quarters monotony, and it pairs beautifully with the abandoned journal as twin pictures of a young man killing time. The draft's "with little else to tell" gestures at the monotony abstractly; the accordion makes it concrete. I'd trade a little of the deserter clause's weight to make room for it.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry passes along a soldier's-eye scrap of intelligence: eight rebels have crossed the lines as deserters, saying the enemy has nothing to eat. The rest is winter-quarters idleness — a borrowed accordion he is learning to play, a journal he has let lapse in the cold — and a quiet wish that he were home for the village sing school.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim checks out against the letter: Camp McClellan, Poolesville about three miles off, eight rebels crossing as deserters reporting the enemy has nothing to eat, the cold-stalled journal he'll be sorry for, and the village sing school he wishes he could attend. Two small accuracy notes, not errors: the recipient is his sister Frances (not a parent), and the letter says he'd "like to attend" the sing school — "give much to be home for" it is a fair, mild amplification but slightly hotter than the source's plainer wistfulness.

FEEDBACK: Strong lead — Confederate hunger on the Potomac, witnessed through eight deserters, is the single most compelling true detail and rightly anchors the summary. The "soldier's-eye glimpse" gloss earns its place. Two issues. First, it runs short of the rich target (~330 chars and reads a touch thin) and leaves on the table the letter's best human texture: this is a bored young man in winter quarters who confesses he had "nothing to write about," is teaching himself the accordion, and can already play the violin. The journal/sing-school beat is good homesickness, but the accordion detail is more vivid and specific. Second, "give much to be home" overstates a quieter line. I'd dial that back and weave in the winter-quarters monotony so the deserter intelligence lands against the dull backdrop that makes it the day's one event. Naming Frances (sister) also adds grounding at no cost.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry has little to report — winter quarters go "on about the same from day to day" — until eight rebels cross the lines as deserters, saying the enemy has nothing to eat: a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac. To fill the cold idle days he is teaching himself the accordion, and admits the journal he let lapse is something he'll be sorry for if he ever gets home.

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is grounded in this letter: Gorman's compliment ("did the best of them all"), the "felt quite proud" quote, the failed attempt to reach Alexander (wrote to Washington per the direction Alexander gave, now hears Washington is wrong), not knowing Alexander's regiment, and the moral commentary on swearing and gambling with the "very strict and firm" quote. Note that the draft renders Gorman's compliment as "judged the 34th New York the best of all regiments at brigade drill" — the letter says Gorman "told our Regiment that they did the best of them all," so "best of all regiments [in the brigade]" is a faithful, not inflated, reading. Good restraint.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and period-accurate. The winter-quarters framing at Camp McClellan is correct (the 34th NY was in Gorman's brigade, Sedgwick's division, near Poolesville that winter), and leading with the brigade-drill compliment is the right anchor — it captures the regimental pride and unit-cohesion-building that defines this lull-period letter. The Alexander thread is the second strongest beat and well-chosen: two soldier-brothers unable to find each other through the mails is exactly the kind of dot a historian connecting the collection wants flagged. Two small notes. First, the middle sentence is slightly tangled ("having written to Washington when that direction proves wrong and Alexander's regiment unknown to him") — it reads a bit clipped and the tense/logic ("when that direction proves wrong") is murky; smooth it. Second, the draft omits the vivid human/disciplinary detail that makes the morals passage land — the four men caught at cards who must stand on a barrel and forfeit wages — and the accidental self-wounding in the Minnesota regiment (the letter's "Wound" flag). You can't fit all of it, but the barrel punishment is the kind of concrete period texture worth trading a few abstract words for. The draft is good as-is; the suggestion below mainly untangles the Alexander clause and adds one concrete beat.

SUGGESTED: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry glows that Gen. Gorman told the 34th New York they "did the best of them all" at brigade drill — "we felt quite proud." Yet he still can't reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington on a direction he now hears is wrong, with Alexander's regiment unknown to him. Disturbed by the camp's swearing and gambling — four men caught at cards must stand on a barrel and forfeit wages — he insists a man keeps good morals there only if "very strict and firm."

FACT ISSUES: none. Every military-relevant claim in the draft is grounded in this letter. Gen. Gorman did compliment the 34th New York at brigade drill ("did the best of them all" → "best of all regiments" is a fair paraphrase); "we felt quite proud" is verbatim; the Alexander address problem (wrote to Washington per the direction Alexander gave, doesn't know his regiment) is accurate; the swearing/gambling commentary and "very strict and firm" quote are verbatim. The draft wisely does NOT import the editorial's outside facts (Baltimore/Camp Jackson, the 60th Regt, the pairing letters) — correctly so, since none of that appears in this letter's text. The "best of all regiments at brigade drill" phrasing is sound: Gorman said the 34th "did the best of them all" after a brigade drill.

FEEDBACK: Military substance is correct and well-emphasized for what this letter actually is — a winter-quarters morale-and-cohesion snapshot, not a combat or movement letter. Leading with Gorman's brigade-drill compliment is the right anchor: it's the concrete unit-cohesion datum a historian wants, and it fixes the 34th NY in winter quarters (Camp McClellan, Poolesville sector) in Dec 1861. Two issues. First, naming the camp "Camp McClellan" without locating it leaves it militarily inert — most readers won't know it's the 34th's Poolesville-area winter camp; either keep it as flavor or let it sit since the letter itself gives no location. Second and more important: the Alexander clause is grammatically muddled — "having written to Washington when that direction proves wrong" reads as a non-sequitur and slightly misstates the sequence. Henry wrote to Washington because that was the direction Alexander gave; he has SINCE heard Washington is wrong and doesn't know the regiment. The draft's tense/causality should be cleaned so the stakes (two soldier-brothers unable to correspond) land clearly. The omitted accidental self-shooting in the Minnesota regiment is a fine cut — minor, and not about Henry's unit. The human beat (pride, then the moral discipline note) is well-chosen and not over-sentimentalized.

SUGGESTED: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry reports that Gen. Gorman judged the 34th New York the best of all regiments at the day's brigade drill — "we felt quite proud," a small index of the cohesion hardening over a winter of drilling. He still cannot reach his brother Alexander: he wrote to Washington as Alexander had directed, only to hear that was the wrong address, and he does not even know Alexander's regiment. Unsettled by the swearing and gambling around him, Henry insists a man can keep good morals in camp only if "very strict and firm."

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is grounded in this letter — the Brigade drill, Gorman's praise that the 34th "did the best of them all," the "we felt quite proud" quote, writing to Alexander at Washington on his own given direction, the rumor that Washington is wrong, not knowing Alexander's regiment, and the swearing/gambling commentary with the "very strict and firm" quote. The draft wisely does NOT import the editorial's outside facts (Baltimore, Camp Jackson, the Minnesota soldier). Note: the draft omits the accidental self-shooting in the Minnesota Regt., which IS in the letter — not an error, but an available beat left on the table.

FEEDBACK: The bones are right and the quotes are honest. But it reads like a competent itemization rather than a scene. Two craft problems. First, the drill sentence is the strongest material — the boy-pride of a green regiment in winter quarters earning a general's nod — yet it's stated and dropped; let it breathe a half-beat. Second, the Alexander passage is the human heart of this letter ("It seems bad that we cannot correspond"), and the draft renders it as a tangle of clauses ("having written to Washington when that direction proves wrong and Alexander's regiment unknown to him") that's grammatically muddy and emotionally cold. That line — two soldier-brothers unable to reach each other across the same war — is the ache. Use it. Also "Disturbed by camp swearing and gambling" is a touch clinical; Henry isn't disturbed so much as bracing himself morally. The three facts don't connect, and they could: pride, isolation, and self-discipline are all one young man taking the measure of camp life.

SUGGESTED: At Camp McClellan in winter quarters, Henry writes home flush with pride: after Brigade drill, Gen. Gorman told the 34th New York "they did the best of them all" — "we felt quite proud, I tell you." But he still cannot reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington as directed only to hear it was the wrong place, and not even knowing Alexander's regiment — "It seems bad that we cannot correspond." Around him the swearing and gambling run so deep, he tells his mother, that a man keeps his morals only "if he is very strict and firm."

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is supported by the letter. Gen. Gorman did say the 34th "did the best of them all" (the draft's "judged the best of all regiments at brigade drill" is a fair paraphrase); "we felt quite proud" is verbatim; Henry wrote to Washington as the direction Alexander gave, now hears it's wrong, and doesn't know Alexander's regiment; the swearing/gambling moral and the "very strict and firm" quote are both exact. Note the draft does NOT import the editorial's outside facts (Baltimore, Camp Jackson, the 40-mile gap) — correctly, since those aren't in this letter. Good discipline.

FEEDBACK: The lead is the right pick — Gorman's compliment and the proud beat is the most vivid, click-worthy true detail, and the verbatim "we felt quite proud" earns its place. The piece is well-structured and lands all three of the letter's strands (pride, the lost-brother problem, the moral commentary). Two issues to sharpen. First, the middle sentence is grammatically tangled: "having written to Washington when that direction proves wrong and Alexander's regiment unknown to him" mixes tenses and reads as a run-on — the "when... proves wrong" clause doesn't parse cleanly. Rewrite as plain cause-and-effect. Second, the draft passes over a small but genuinely human/historical detail that adds texture for nearly free: the dictionary he plans to buy in Washington and send home — a quiet domestic note of self-improvement that sits in nice tension with the swearing-and-gambling moral. Optional, but it sharpens the "upright soldier" through-line. Length is fine; tightening the middle sentence frees room.

SUGGESTED: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry reports that Gen. Gorman told the 34th New York they "did the best of them all" at brigade drill — "we felt quite proud," he writes. Still unable to reach his brother Alexander, whose regiment he doesn't know and whose Washington address he now hears is wrong, he turns to the camp's swearing and gambling, insisting a young man can keep good morals there only if "very strict and firm."

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim is anchored in the letter: Camp McClellan as the dateline, the long-awaited word from Alexander, the misdirected letter ("not quite correct" direction), Capt. Ransom's narrow escape relayed via Alex, the stove, barracks-building, the $25 promised next pay day, and the self-conscious apology about spelling and "writing in a hurry." Names, sums, and the unit context are preserved accurately.

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, vivid draft that earns its length and lands squarely in the target voice. The anchor is well chosen — for a historian connecting the collection's dots, the load-bearing fact is that Henry, the first brother in uniform, is straining to keep the family network intact across distance, and the news of Capt. Ransom's escape is the period-correct hook (an officer of Henry's company brushing danger, conveyed third-hand through a brother). My one substantive note: the summary slightly buries Ransom. A narrow escape by a company captain is the sharpest "why this matters" thread for a war historian, yet it sits in a subordinate clause mid-sentence. Consider giving it a touch more prominence, since outcomes and named officers are exactly what a researcher cross-references. The human beat (the spelling apology to a mother "who reads every line") is woven, not tacked on, and tonally right — warm without sentimentality. Two small economy notes: "stove-buying, barracks-building" is a pleasing cadence but flirts with the banned bare topic-list rhythm; and "at last heard from" plus "letter reached camp despite a direction that was not quite correct" is mildly redundant since both describe the same delayed-mail event. Period framing is sound — "next pay day" and remitting wages home are authentic to a private's correspondence. No changes are strictly required; the draft is publishable as is.

SUGGESTED: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry — the first of the brothers in uniform — finally has word from Alexander, a letter that reached camp despite a slightly wrong direction, and through it the news that Capt. Ransom had a narrow escape. Between buying a stove, raising barracks, and promising to send $25 home next pay day, he sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.

FACT ISSUES: none. The unit reference ("send $25 home next pay day"), Camp McClellan, Capt. Ransom's "narrow escape," Alexander, the stove, and the barracks construction are all directly supported. The draft correctly avoids importing outside facts (e.g., it does not name the boiler-explosion detail or the 40-mile separation, which appear only in the editorial layer, not this letter's text). The "$25" and "next pay day" are both literal. Good restraint.

FEEDBACK: Militarily the draft is clean and accurate — no unit/rank/date errors, and nothing overstated. One note from my lens: the letter is unusually rich in concrete military-camp texture that the draft underuses. The most period-evocative operational details — Henry's company coming off a 24-hour picket on Christmas morning, and the regiment having barracks built (the shift into formal winter quarters) — are stronger "historian's hooks" than stove-buying, because they mark the campaign rhythm of a regiment settling in for winter 1861-62. The draft mentions barracks-building only in a domestic-sounding cluster ("stove-buying, barracks-building"), which flattens a real military milestone into housekeeping. The Ransom "narrow escape" is well-handled (teased, not spoiled). The Alexander reconnection is correctly identified as the anchor. Consider promoting the picket duty and winter-quarters framing so the military substance leads and the spelling beat stays as the human close. The draft is also slightly long on the spelling vow relative to its payoff.

SUGGESTED: From Camp McClellan over Christmas 1861 — his company just off a 24-hour picket on Christmas morning, the regiment's winter barracks going up — Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from his brother Alexander, whose misdirected letter found camp anyway, and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between buying a sheet-iron stove and promising $25 home next pay day, he sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, knowing she reads every line.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is grounded in the letter: Camp McClellan as the dateline, the long-awaited letter from Alexander, the "not quite correct" direction that arrived anyway, Alex's report that Capt. Ransom had a "narrow escape," the sheet-iron stove, barracks being built for the regiment, the promise to send $25 home next pay day, and Henry's vow to mind his spelling because he "sometimes" writes "in a hurry." All accurate, all from this page.

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, warm draft with a genuine McCullough cadence — and the instinct to lead with the reunion is exactly right, because reconnecting with Alexander is the historically load-bearing fact a reader tracing the brothers' threads must catch. Two notes. First, a small precision matter: the draft says Henry "writing in a hurry" as if it's his settled habit, but the letter is gentler and more self-aware — he confesses he writes hurriedly "sometimes" and resolves to "be more careful after this." The current phrasing slightly overstates; the truer beat is the resolution, the boyish promise to do better. Second, "a mother he knows reads every line" is a lovely touch but it's an inference the letter doesn't quite make — Henry never says she reads carefully; that's editorial license. It reads beautifully, but under the no-invention rule I'd anchor it to something he does say. The middle clause — "stove-buying, barracks-building" — is crisp and earns its keep. Overall the draft is close to shippable; I'd tighten the two soft spots rather than rebuild.

SUGGESTED: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from Alexander — the letter reached camp despite a direction "not quite correct" — and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between buying a sheet-iron stove against the cold and the barracks rising for his regiment, he promises to send $25 home next pay day, then sheepishly vows to mind his spelling and "be more careful after this."

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim checks against the letter — Camp McClellan, the long-awaited word from Alexander, the address that was "not quite correct," Alex's report of Capt. Ransom's narrow escape, the stove, barracks work, the $25 promised next pay day, and the self-conscious apology for spelling and haste. Confirm Ransom's spelling and the "$25"/"next pay day" phrasing match the transcription exactly as rendered.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and earns its length. The lead is well chosen — finally hearing from Alexander is the genuine historical hook (an inter-brother communication node a researcher tracing the family network wants flagged), and the Ransom near-miss rides in naturally as the payload of that letter. The closing human beat (sheepishly minding his spelling for a mother who "reads every line") lands warmly without tipping into sentiment. Two small tightenings: "stove-buying, barracks-building" is a near-miss topic-list rhythm — it reads as a paired gerund list rather than prose; consider reframing one as a clause. And "a direction that was 'not quite correct'" is slightly clinical; "direction" for a mailing address may read oddly to a modern eye, though the quoted phrase is faithful. Minor only — the draft is publishable close to as-is.

SUGGESTED: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from Alexander — the letter reached camp despite an address "not quite correct" — and passes along Alex's word that Capt. Ransom had a narrow escape. Between buying a stove and helping raise the barracks, he promises to send $25 home next pay day, then sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.

critiques.text:
FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is grounded in this letter: Camp McClellan; New Year's beer "from the Capt." with some boys drunk; the company presenting Capt. Reich a $125 sword; Henry's $1 contribution; the furlough longing limited to married men; the loneliness/want of letters; and the box of socks stuck in Washington. No imported events, units, or names. (Minor framing note: "a dollar on a private's pay" is an editorial gloss — the letter never states Henry's rank — but it is a defensible characterization for a Co. D enlisted man and not a factual overreach.)

FEEDBACK: This is a strong, vivid draft that earns its length and stays period-correct. The sword presentation is rightly the anchor — a $125 ornamental officer's sword bought by pooled enlisted contributions is exactly the unit-cohesion ritual a historian wants flagged, and the $1-against-a-private's-pay detail lands the human/economic stake well. The furlough-only-for-married-men line is a genuinely valuable period detail and a good human beat. Two thoughts. First, the draft opens on the beer/drunkenness, which is colorful but the least historically load-bearing fact; consider leading harder on the sword so the anchor isn't buried behind the carousing. Second, the letter has a richer texture you're leaving on the table — the Minnesota band playing before the Colonel's tent all New Year's night (a nice marker of inter-regimental sociability in Gorman's brigade) — though space is tight and the socks/furlough beats already carry the homesickness. The draft is good enough that changes are optional polish, not correction.

SUGGESTED: On New Year's at Camp McClellan, Henry's company presented Capt. Reich a handsome $125 sword — Henry giving a dollar toward it on a soldier's pay — while a Minnesota band played before the Colonel's tent and a few of the boys, glad of the Captain's beer, drank more than was necessary. He longs for a furlough home, but only married men may go, so he waits — lonesome for letters, the box of socks still stuck in Washington.

FACT ISSUES: none. The letter places Henry at Camp McClellan; the company's presentation of a $125 sword to Capt. Reich, Henry's one-dollar contribution on a private's pay, the New Year's beer "from the Capt.," the few drunk boys, the furlough restricted to married men, the lonesomeness for letters, and the box of socks stuck in Washington are all grounded in the transcription. No units, dates, ranks, movements, or outcomes are misstated or invented. (Note: the draft does not name Henry's regiment, the 34th NY — that is acceptable, since the summary should only carry what this letter states, and the letter itself does not name the unit.)

FEEDBACK: From a military lens this is clean and accurate — no false unit/rank/movement claims, and the one military-adjacent detail that matters (a company subscription buying a presentation sword for the captain, a common ritual of unit cohesion and officer esteem in 1861-62 volunteer regiments) is correctly framed. The "$125 sword / a dollar on a private's pay" contrast is the strongest historical-human hook and is well chosen; it quietly conveys the economic gulf between officers and enlisted men. The draft earns its length and stays vivid. My only substantive note: this is a winter-camp morale-and-logistics letter, not an operational one, and the summary correctly resists inflating it. Minor polish — "a few boys too drunk" reads slightly clipped, and "to which he gave a dollar" is mildly ambiguous (Henry gave the dollar, not Reich). Worth tightening the sword clause so the subject is unmistakable.

SUGGESTED: From Camp McClellan, Henry rings in the new year with beer "from the Capt." and a few boys gone drunk, then reports his company chipped in to present Capt. Reich a $125 sword — Henry's own share a hard-found dollar on a private's pay. Minor, but it slightly oversteps. "beer 'from the Capt.'" — supported. "a few boys too drunk" — supported ("Some of the boys got drunk"). "only married men may go" — supported. "lonesome for letters" — supported ("I get very lonesome if I do not get a paper or something else to read"). "box of socks still stuck in Washington" — supported ("The box of socks has not arrived yet. I expect the box is in Washington"). FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim in the draft is grounded in this letter: the dateline "Camp McClellan," the recipient being his sister Frances, the burning of all letters received from home, the knapsack-space rationale, the verbatim "if I should go over into Virginia," the verbatim P.S. "Please burn all my letters," and the closing line that he is glad for her sake she is going to teach in Montreal this winter. The draft does not import outside events. (One light note: the letter says "I received a letter from Nellie and Aunt Laura," so the burned home letters and his continuing receipt of mail coexist — the draft doesn't misstate this, but it is worth knowing the burning was not a total cutoff.)

FEEDBACK: This is strong, period-correct, and historically alert. The draft correctly identifies the postscript as the gravitational center — the request that, had Frances obeyed, would have erased the very collection a reader is browsing. That is exactly the "stake" a historian connecting the dots must take away, and the draft teases it without over-explaining. The mirrored framing (Henry burns incoming letters / asks Frances to burn his outgoing) is elegant and faithful. Two refinements from my lens: (1) The summary leaves the soldier's-anxiety reading implicit. The phrase "if I should go over into Virginia" is the period-correct tell — a Co. D man at winter camp anticipating the move south, where letters on a body were a liability. A light contextual touch there would deepen the "why it matters" without spoiling. (2) The Montreal teaching detail, while accurate, is the least consequential fact and currently gets a full closing sentence equal in weight to the burn request; it reads slightly tacked-on. I'd either subordinate it or trim it so the editorial energy stays on the correspondence's near-destruction. The draft is well within the 350-450 target and earns its length.

SUGGESTED: Writing to his sister Frances from winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry reports he has burned every letter he received from home — they crowded his knapsack, and he did not want them on him "if I should go over into Virginia." Then the postscript turns the request back on her: "Please burn all my letters." Had Frances obeyed, the very correspondence we now read would not survive. He closes, almost lightly, glad for her sake that she will teach in Montreal this winter.

FACT ISSUES: none. Camp McClellan, sister Frances, the burning of received letters, the "if I should go over into Virginia" line, the "Please burn all my letters" postscript, and Frances teaching in Montreal are all drawn from this letter. No unit, rank, date, or movement is asserted, so nothing is misstated. Worth noting for context: Camp McClellan (near Camp California, Alexandria, VA) was the 34th NY's winter-1861-62 encampment, and the "go over into Virginia" line is the letter's one genuine military signal — Henry is on the Maryland/D.C. side anticipating a forward movement across the Potomac into Virginia. The draft carries that line but doesn't frame its significance.

FEEDBACK: The draft is accurate and the letter-burning motif is well chosen — it's the human core and reads vividly. But from a military lens the summary slightly buries the one fact a historian tracing the 34th NY's movements would seize on: the burning isn't just decluttering, it's a soldier stripping his pack in anticipation of crossing into Virginia, i.e. the army's expected advance from winter quarters. The draft quotes that line but treats it as a parenthetical reason for the burning; it could be elevated to read as the operational anticipation it is. The Montreal clause is fine as the closing human beat but is the least important fact and eats characters — trim or keep it brief. Length is in good range; tighten the middle to let the Virginia anticipation land.

FEEDBACK: This is strong work; it already finds the letter's quiet drama. The burned letters are the right anchor, and the mirrored postscript ("Please burn all my letters") is exactly the kind of detail that turns a soldier's housekeeping into something that catches in the throat — a young man clearing himself of anything that could be found on his body across the river. What I would adjust is the architecture: the draft front-loads the mechanics ("they crowded his knapsack") before the stake, slightly burying the emotional charge of Virginia. Lead with the act and the dread, let the practical reason follow, and let the Montreal note land as the human grace-note it is — a brother who, even while contemplating his own mortality, is glad for his sister's small forward step. Tighten "turns the request around," which reads a touch mechanical for so charged a reversal.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim checks out against the letter — the position "within five miles of Richmond," the June 16 dating tied to the regiment having been "mustered into the U.S. service one year ago this day," the count of "less than five hundred men fit for duty," the week under the doctor's care, the captured rebel's remark on the speed of Yankee loading and firing, and the ladies' carriages that came expecting to ride into a Union defeat and were turned to hauling off Confederate wounded.

The structure is sound: the anniversary-and-attrition anchor lands the historical stakes first (a regiment one year old already worn down to fewer than five hundred fit men, five miles from the rebel capital), then the captured-rebel anecdote delivers the human and ironic texture. My only quibble is one of rhythm and emphasis. The phrase "Recovering from a week under the doctor's care" sits as a flat aside between two stronger beats and slightly mutes the momentum; Henry's own convalescence is the most personal thread here, and it deserves either fuller weight or a lighter touch rather than a parenthetical shrug. And "jokes that" undersells the closing image — the irony is grim and self-aware, and naming it a joke flattens it. Let the picture do the work. Trust the carriages.

FACT ISSUES: none. Every claim is grounded in the letter: writing to brother Charles from camp near Richmond; the regiment "pushed right in head first"; halting to fire low into kneeling rebels before they could deliver their volley; the Colonel's reckoning of three hundred killed and wounded; the confidential "almost tempted to desert sometimes," checked by disgrace and by his mother being alone; and Capt. Reich put in irons and discharged for refusing an order. No outside events (Seven Days, Fair Oaks, etc.) are imported, and no dates, names, or units are invented or misstated.

FEEDBACK: This is strong and well within the rich target length. The anchor is correctly the combat narrative, and the historian's payoff — the private desertion confession Henry entrusts to one brother and no one else — is exactly the right human beat to surface; it captures the gap between a soldier's public posture and his interior state in mid-1862. The framing is period-correct: firing low into kneeling infantry, the disgrace of desertion as a check, and an officer ironed and cashiered for insubordination are all idiomatically of the war. One judgment call: the Reich detail, while accurate, reads as a third appended fact and slightly dilutes the through-line of the letter, which is Henry's combat experience and his confession. If trimmed or compressed it tightens the arc; if kept, it's defensible as texture about discipline in the ranks. Minor: "by his Colonel's account three hundred dead and wounded" is good, but making clear this is the regiment's tally vs. the enemy's would sharpen it — the letter attributes the rebel casualties to the charge, so "rebel dead and wounded" avoids ambiguity. Optional polish below; the draft is publishable as-is.

To Charles alone he confesses he is "almost tempted to desert sometimes," held back only by the disgrace and by his mother left all alone — even as Capt. Reich is put in irons and discharged for refusing an order.
